sections.p02.s0: Work in order: iterators, then generators, lazy pipelines and itertools, then the object-model traps (identity, hashing, default arguments). Spend about three days on the reading and REPL exercises and two on the multi-GB file build, which uses everything before it.
sections.p02.s1: Do decorators and context managers first (about two days), then type hints and a full type-checker run (two days), and finish with the module refactor. The refactored project is a good base for the engineering challenge that follows.
sections.p02.s2: One refactor of File Organizer, done in this order: split the four layers, share one code path for dry-run and execute, then write the disk-free tests, which prove the redesign worked. Plan about a week; most of it goes on the split.

p02.s0.0.how: Write a class Countdown whose __iter__ returns self and whose __next__ counts n down to 1, then raises StopIteration. Drive it by hand with iter() and next(), then with a for loop. Then write an iterable whose __iter__ returns a new iterator each time.
p02.s0.0.done: You can explain the difference between an iterable and an iterator, and why a second for loop over the same iterator prints nothing.

p02.s0.1.how: Rewrite Countdown as a generator function and compare the line count. Write the same thing as a generator expression, then a generator that delegates to two sub-generators with yield from. Put a print before each yield to see when the body actually runs.
p02.s0.1.done: You can say why a generator object can only be iterated once and at what moment its body code runs.

p02.s0.2.how: Build a chain of generator functions, read_lines then parse then keep_errors then count_by_key, each taking an iterable and yielding. Run it on a large log file, then write a version that builds a list at every stage and compare peak memory.
p02.s0.2.done: Each stage can be tested alone on a three-item list, and the full pipeline holds about one line in memory at a time.

p02.s0.3.how: Try islice, chain, groupby and tee in the REPL on small lists. Run groupby on unsorted input to see it only groups consecutive keys, then sort first. Take the first 10 lines of a file with islice instead of reading it into a list.
p02.s0.3.done: You can predict the output of groupby on unsorted data and explain why tee can use a lot of memory.

p02.s0.4.how: In the REPL compare is and == on lists, small ints and strings, and check id(). Write a class with __eq__ but no __hash__ and try to add it to a set. Then use a tuple that contains a list as a dict key and read the error.
p02.s0.4.done: You can explain why a key that changes after insertion breaks dict lookup, and why defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None.

p02.s0.5.how: Write def add(item, bucket=[]), call it three times and print the result. Fix it with a None sentinel. Then reproduce two more shared-state traps: a list as a class attribute shared by all instances, and a grid built with [[0] * 3] * 3.
p02.s0.5.done: You can explain that default values are evaluated once, when def runs, and spot the bug in someone else's code.

p02.s0.6.how: Generate a test file of several GB. Write a one-pass generator pipeline that aggregates it. Measure peak memory with tracemalloc.get_traced_memory() (or the process peak in Task Manager) on a 100 MB and a multi-GB input, then write the list-based version and measure it too.
p02.s0.6.done: Peak memory is about the same for the 100 MB and multi-GB inputs, and both numbers are written down next to the list version's.

p02.s1.0.how: Write each decorator as a function returning a wrapper: timer using time.perf_counter, retry that re-calls on an exception with doubling sleeps, logger that logs arguments and return value, cache that stores results in a dict keyed on the arguments. Test each one.
p02.s1.0.done: You can write timer from a blank file and explain that @timer means f = timer(f).

p02.s1.1.how: Print __name__ and __doc__ of a decorated function with and without @functools.wraps. Then turn retry into retry(times=3, delay=0.5), which needs three nested functions: the factory, the decorator and the wrapper.
p02.s1.1.done: You can explain why a decorator that takes arguments needs one more level of nesting than one that does not.

p02.s1.2.how: Write a Timer class with __enter__ and __exit__ that records elapsed time, then the same with @contextlib.contextmanager using try/finally around yield. Raise an exception inside the with block and check that cleanup still runs in both.
p02.s1.2.done: Cleanup runs when the body raises, and you can say what returning True from __exit__ does to the exception.

p02.s1.3.how: Annotate one small module using each feature at least once: X | None returns, a Protocol argument, Self on a builder method, @override in a subclass, a TypedDict record, a PEP 695 generic function and a type alias. Run a type checker on it.
p02.s1.3.done: The module type-checks clean, and a deliberately wrong call against each annotation is reported by the checker.

p02.s1.4.how: Install mypy and run it on a project from an earlier phase. Start with default settings, fix errors one file at a time, then turn on --strict for one module. Keep a list of real bugs found versus missing-annotation noise.
p02.s1.4.done: The checker exits with zero errors on the project, and you can name at least one real bug it caught.

p02.s1.5.how: Pick an earlier project and draw its modules and which imports which. Move code so that I/O, core logic and the CLI sit in separate modules and the core imports neither of the others. Import each module on its own to check for cycles.
p02.s1.5.done: Each module has one stated job, nothing has an import cycle, and the core module imports nothing from the CLI or I/O code.

p02.s2.0.how: Write classify() as a pure function that takes plain data (name, suffix, size, modified time) and returns a destination, with no os, shutil or Path I/O calls. The scanner builds that data and a separate mover acts on the result.
p02.s2.0.done: You can call classify() in the REPL with hand-made inputs while no test directory exists anywhere.

p02.s2.1.how: Make four modules: rules.py (pure decisions), fs.py (scan, move, mkdir), config.py (load and validate settings into a dataclass) and cli.py, which wires them together. Only cli.py configures logging; the others call logging.getLogger(__name__).
p02.s2.1.done: rules.py imports nothing from the other three modules and contains no open(, shutil or os calls.

p02.s2.2.how: Make the planner return a list of planned moves (source, destination). Execute mode hands that list to an executor that moves files; dry-run hands it to one that only logs. Add a --dry-run flag with argparse.
p02.s2.2.done: Dry-run and execute log the same plan for the same folder, and after a dry-run the folder is unchanged.

p02.s2.3.how: Write pytest tests that feed the planner lists of fake file records and assert on the returned moves: name clashes, unknown suffixes, duplicates, empty input. Add a fixture that uses monkeypatch to make shutil.move and Path.iterdir raise, so any disk access fails the test.
p02.s2.3.done: The decision tests pass with the disk-access guard active and the whole file runs in under a second.
